title-group.article-title: Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation on a Laptop: A Native MLX Study of Next-Concept Modeling

abstract.p: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) generates a sequence through successive levels of discrete latent codes, predicting each level in parallel. We independently implement the method in MLX and study synthetic language and Sudoku on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs. On a finite synthetic grammar, a 5M-parameter generator achieves lower small-batch latency than a similarly sized autoregressive generator, with lower sentence validity (89.8% versus 98.6%). Two Sudoku training seeds use the same 6.44M-parameter generator recipe and 16.384M presentations each. Retained greedy evaluation aggregates report easy/medium/hard solve rates of 98.10/83.40/40.30% for seed 0 and 97.25/79.60/33.25% for seed 1, with 2,000 boards per difficulty. The hard-set difference is 7.05 percentage points; two seeds do not establish population training variability or its cause. Original NCM reports 99.50/96.50/86.10% with a 25.46M generator, 51.2M presentations and a different task setup. Our generator is 3.95 times smaller, excluding its additional codec; the comparison establishes neither task parity nor matched-cost efficiency. E20 completes its schedule without a recorded reset or truncation, but missing per-board predictions and remote provenance manifests limit independent audit. We characterize this phase as a partial implementation and small-model success, retain the substantial hard-Sudoku deficit, and define controlled text evaluation as the next research direction rather than a demonstrated capability.

disp-quote.p: Status. Working paper, version 0.11. Every number here is copied from a run in the code repository (runs/, summarised in paper/data/results.json) or quoted from the cited paper and marked as quoted. Experiments still running are marked in progress and never estimated. Appendix C lists the changes between versions.

sec.title: Reading guide
sec.p: This paper has two audiences. If you are new to language models, read Section 2 (the idea in plain language) and Section 3 (glossary), then the boxed summary at the start of each later section. If you build models, Sections 5–7 give the method with every formula explained, the Apple Silicon implementation and the experiments. Section 8 tells the story of the project run by run: what each experiment (E0, E1, …) asked, what changed and what we learned.

sec.title: How a chat model writes
sec.p: A chat model such as ChatGPT or Qwen writes one token (a word or a piece of a word) at a time. To write the 100th token it runs the whole model once, reads what it has written so far and picks the next token. A 100-token answer therefore needs 100 full runs of the model, one after the other. At small batch sizes, autoregressive decoding often spends much of its time moving model weights from memory. The balance depends on the model, hardware, cache and implementation; these experiments measure latency, not memory-bandwidth utilisation.

sec.title: How next-concept modeling writes
sec.p: NCM (Kumbong et al. 2026) writes differently. It first produces a single, very rough “concept” for the whole text, then refines it in a few rounds. Each round adds roughly twice as much detail, and every piece of detail in a round is produced at the same time. Figure 1 shows a real example from this project: a 32-character sentence written in six rounds (levels). After level 0 the rough shape is there (“eue likes one oed egg.”); by level 2 the words are settled; later levels only change single letters.

caption.p: A real generation from experiment E1. Left: the codes of each level; all codes in one row come from one model run. Right: the text obtained by decoding everything up to that level. Six model runs write the sentence; a word-by-word model needs 32. The sample also shows a failure: level 3 turns “red” into “ret”, and nothing later repairs it.

sec.p: The number of rounds is fixed by the model configuration (six in TinyWorld, twelve in the original paper’s Sudoku model), so NCM needs far fewer model runs than a word-by-word model. That is where its speed comes from.

sec.title: Two parts: a codec and a generator
sec.p: NCM has two learned parts. An analogy from image files helps.

list-item.p: The codec is like an image format with progressive loading: a JPEG that first shows a blurry picture, then sharpens. It learns to turn a sentence into a stack of codes, from one coarse code to one code per letter, and to turn the codes back into the sentence. It is trained first, on its own, with reconstruction losses. Full-hierarchy reconstruction is measured separately from generation quality.
The generator is the creative part. It learns to invent new code stacks one level at a time: level 0, then level 1 given level 0, and so on. The codec then turns the finished stack into text.

sec.title: Why it matters, and the catch
sec.p: Fewer, wider model runs suit a laptop GPU: one run reads the weights once and does a lot of arithmetic with them. The catch is that all codes of a level are chosen at the same moment, so neighbouring pieces cannot see each other’s choice. If two pieces of a level disagree, the result can be wrong in a way a word-by-word model would avoid. Much of this paper measures when that matters.

sec.title: What we did
sec.p: We rebuilt NCM from scratch for Apple’s MLX framework (Hannun et al. 2023), tested it on a small invented language and on Sudoku puzzles (the original paper’s showcase), and compared it with a character-level AR model of similar generator size and with a large chat model. The speed advantage holds on a laptop. On Sudoku, two training seeds solve 97.25–98.10% of easy boards but only 33.25–40.30% of hard boards. Original NCM reports 99.5% and 86.1%, respectively, under a different setup. A historical comparison matches generator presentations against our AR baseline; Section 8 records the experiments. NCM is a generation method used here for two tasks, not a Sudoku-specific expansion of the term or an instruction-following language model.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Residual vector quantisation. A vector quantiser maps a continuous vector to the nearest of V V codebook entries (Oord et al. 2017). Residual quantisation applies several quantisers in sequence, each to what the previous ones left over (Lee et al. 2022; Zeghidour et al. 2021); it underlies modern neural audio codecs.

Next-scale prediction. VAR (Tian et al. 2024) combines residual quantisation with resolution: the first quantiser sees a 1\times1 1×1 summary of an image, later ones 2\times2 2×2,
3\times3 3×3, up to full resolution, and a transformer generates one scale per step. NCM applies the idea to 1-D token sequences (Kumbong et al. 2026).

Diffusion language models refine positions of a sequence over T T denoising steps (Sahoo et al. 2024). Full-sequence samplers process length
L L at each step; NCM’s early levels process fewer code positions, although prefix and decoder work also contribute. The NCM paper reports quality at or above strong diffusion language models with 10–31× faster generation under its H100 benchmark protocol (Kumbong et al. 2026).

sec.title: Method

disp-quote.p: In short. The codec learns to describe a sequence with a stack of codes, coarse to fine. The generator learns to predict each level’s codes from the levels above it. Generation runs the generator once per level, then decodes.

sec.p:
We follow the NCM design (Kumbong et al. 2026) and its released Sudoku configuration; Table 2 lists where we differ. A running toy example uses a sequence of
L = 8 L=8 tokens, levels l = (1, 2, 4, 8) l=(1,2,4,8) and vectors of width C = 2 C=2.

sec.title: Codec: from tokens to a stack of codes
sec.p: Encoder. Each token x_i xi and its position i i are looked up in two tables, added and normalised:

Reading it: W_{\mathrm{tok}} Wtok has one learned row per possible token and
W_{\mathrm{pos}} Wpos one per position; z z is the whole sequence as L L vectors of C C numbers. “Norm” rescales each vector (LayerNorm), or groups of channels across the sequence (GroupNorm, as upstream), without a learned scale, because the quantiser compares squared distances and a learned scale could grow without bound. In the toy example
z z is an 8 \times 2 8×2 table of numbers.
Quantisation, level by level. The quantiser keeps a residual r r, initially all of z z, and for each level k = 0, \dots, K-1 k=0,…,K−1 does four things:

alternatives.tex-math: \underbrace{x_k = D_k\, r_k}_{\text{1. shrink}} ,\qquad \underbrace{c_k = \arg\min_j \lVert x_k - E_k[j] \rVert^2}_{\text{2. pick nearest codes}},
\underbrace{q_k = \phi_k\big(U_k\, E_k[c_k]\big)}_{\text{3. expand and refine}},\qquad \underbrace{r_{k+1} = r_k - \mathrm{sg}(q_k)}_{\text{4. subtract}} .

list-item.p: Shrink. D_k Dk averages the residual down to l_k lk positions (area pooling). Toy example: for level 1 ( l_1 = 2 l1=2), positions 1–4 are averaged into one vector and 5–8 into another.

Pick. For each of the
l_k lk shrunk vectors, find the nearest of the
V V codebook entries E_k[1..V] Ek[1..V]; its index is the code. c_k ck is a list of l_k lk integers, for example (5, 12) (5,12).

Expand and refine. Look the codes back up, stretch them to L L positions by linear interpolation ( U_k Uk), and apply \phi_k(h) = (1-\rho)\,h + \rho\,\mathrm{conv}_k(h) ϕk(h)=(1−ρ)h+ρconvk(h): a small learned convolution blended half and half ( \rho = 0.5 ρ=0.5) with its input, which smooths the blocky stretched result.

Subtract. Remove what this level explained, so the next level only describes what is left.
\mathrm{sg} sg (stop-gradient) means the subtraction is not differentiated.

sec.p: The reconstruction after level k k is the sum of everything explained so far:

alternatives.tex-math: \hat z_k = \sum_{j \le k} q_j, \qquad \hat z = \hat z_{K-1} \approx z .

sec.p: Decoding \hat z_k ẑk for k < K-1 k<K−1 gives the “after level k k” texts of Figure 1.
Codebook updates. Codebooks are not trained by gradients. After each step every entry moves towards the average of the vectors assigned to it:

alternatives.tex-math: N_j \leftarrow \gamma N_j + (1-\gamma)\, n_j, \qquad m_j \leftarrow \gamma m_j + (1-\gamma) \sum_{i:\,c_i = j} x_i, \qquad E[j] = m_j / \tilde N_j .

sec.p:
Reading it: n_j nj counts how many vectors picked entry j j in this batch, N_j Nj is its running average with decay \gamma = 0.99 γ=0.99,
m_j mj the running sum of those vectors, and \tilde N_j Ñj is N_j Nj with a tiny amount added to every count (Laplace smoothing) so nothing is divided by zero. Entries nobody uses ( N_j Nj below a threshold) restart at a random input vector.

Losses. The decoder, one transformer block, reads
\tilde z = z + \mathrm{sg}(\hat z - z) z̃=z+sg(ẑ−z). Numerically this is \hat z ẑ, but its gradient flows into z z as if quantisation were the identity (the straight-through estimator), so the encoder learns. The training loss is

alternatives.tex-math: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{codec}} = \underbrace{\mathrm{CE}\big(\mathrm{Dec}(\tilde z), x\big)}_{\text{rebuild the tokens}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_k \Big(\beta\,\lVert \mathrm{sg}(\hat z_k) - z\rVert^2 + \lVert \hat z_k - \mathrm{sg}(z) \rVert^2\Big)}_{\text{VQ loss}}, \quad \beta = 0.25 .

sec.p:
Reading it: the first term asks the decoder to rebuild the exact tokens. The commitment term ( \beta β) pulls the encoder output towards what the codes can express; the fit term trains the refinement convolutions
\phi_k ϕk so each partial sum \hat z_k ẑk is as close to z z as possible.

Fine-level dropout. Half of the time the decoder receives \hat z_k ẑk for a random k < K-1 k<K−1 instead of the full \hat z ẑ. It must then make sense of a coarse-only description, which is why every prefix of levels decodes to a plausible sequence: a form of nested dropout (Rippel et al. 2014).

Learned level 0. Averaging an entire Sudoku grid into one vector gives nearly the same vector for every grid, so level 0 carries no information (Section 7.2). Upstream replaces
D_0 D0 and U_0 U0 by a strided convolution and a transposed convolution initialised to behave like pooling and repetition. Picking a code has no gradient, so the gradient reaches them through a straight-through estimator:
q_0 q0 is built from x_0 + \mathrm{sg}(E_0[c_0] - x_0) x0+sg(E0[c0]−x0), whose value is the code vector and whose gradient is that of
x_0 x0.

sec.title: Generator: predicting one level from the levels above
sec.p: The generator is a transformer that reads one long row of vectors:

Reading it: the prefix holds the conditioning, for Sudoku the 81 cells of the puzzle (blanks as 0). Level 0 has nothing above it, so it reads learned query vectors. Every other level reads the reconstruction from all coarser levels, shrunk to its own length. Toy example:
\mathrm{input}_2 input2 is \hat z_1 ẑ1 (levels 0 and 1 combined) averaged down to 4 positions. Head
k k turns each of the l_k lk positions of its block into a probability for each of the
V V codes of level k k.

Training loss. With the true codes
c_k ck of a training example,

Reading it: \mathrm{CE}_k CEk is the average surprise at the true codes of level
k k; weighting by l_k lk makes every code count equally (the paper’s
\alpha = 0 α=0 setting (Kumbong et al. 2026, App. F.2.3)). A uniform guess among 16 codes scores \ln 16 \approx 2.77 ln⁡16≈2.77.

Attention pattern. Positions of level
k k may read the prefix and the other positions of level
k k, nothing else (block-diagonal attention); coarser levels reach level k k only through \mathrm{input}_k inputk. Two consequences follow. Training on the whole row at once computes exactly what level-by-level generation computes (tested, Section 6.2). And each level’s codes are chosen without seeing each other’s choices, the source of both the speed and errors like “red” → “ret”. RoPE (Su et al. 2021) positions restart at zero in every level, a learned level embedding tells levels apart, and queries and keys are RMS-normalised.

Conditioning corruption. In training the generator reads true coarser codes; in generation it reads its own, sometimes wrong, codes. Upstream narrows this gap by replacing a fraction
p_k pk of the conditioning codes of level k k with random codes of the same level, keeping the true codes as targets, with p_k pk falling linearly across levels (Kumbong et al. 2026, Sec. 3.4):

This is the coarse-to-fine analogue of scheduled sampling (Bengio et al. 2015). The paper notes that corruption “based on the model’s actual errors may better match inference conditions” but does not test it; experiment E9 tests it and finds no gain at our scale (Section 8).

sec.title: Generation
sec.p:
For k = 0, \dots, K-1 k=0,…,K−1: run the generator on \mathrm{input}_k inputk and the prefix, sample all l_k lk codes of level k k at once, add their contribution q_k qk to the reconstruction and shrink it into
\mathrm{input}_{k+1} inputk+1. Finally decode \hat z_{K-1} ẑK−1 to tokens. Cost: K K generator passes and one decoder pass, independent of how long each level is.

caption.p: Initial E6 settings versus released Original NCM Sudoku settings (Kumbong et al. 2026, Tables 5–6). Later runs change exposure and corruption; see Appendix A.

disp-quote.p: In short. Pure MLX and NumPy, no code copied from upstream. Two findings matter beyond this project: Apple GPUs compute fp32 matrix products at reduced precision, and block-diagonal attention is faster computed per level than through a mask.

sec.title: Framework mapping
sec.p:
Codebooks and their running averages are frozen MLX arrays updated outside automatic differentiation; the shrink and stretch operators D_k Dk,
U_k Uk are precomputed matrices; attention uses MLX’s fused scaled_dot_product_attention. Weights are stored as safetensors. The correspondence to upstream is documented component by component in docs/research/upstream-map.md.

sec.title: Exactness and Metal precision
sec.p: A test asserts that level-by-level generation produces the same logits as the training forward. On the Metal GPU the two disagreed by about 5 \times 10^{-4} 5×10−4. Against a float64 NumPy reference, the same fp32 computation had an error of 1.4 \times 10^{-2} 1.4×10−2 on the GPU and 2 \times 10^{-6} 2×10−6 on the CPU: fp32 matrix products on Metal run at reduced internal precision, about 10^{-3} 10−3 relative. Exactness tests therefore run on the CPU, and a separate test checks the GPU path within 5 \times 10^{-3} 5×10−3. This matters for anyone writing equivalence tests for MLX models; sampling quality is evaluated separately, and these exactness checks do not establish the quality effect of precision.

sec.title: Segmented block-diagonal attention
sec.p:
With a mask, attention over the full Sudoku row forms a
395 \times 395 395×395 score matrix per head, most of it masked out. Computing attention separately for the prefix and for each level (keys and values: prefix plus that level) gives the same result with
P^2 + \sum_k l_k (P + l_k) \approx 48{,}000 P2+∑klk(P+lk)≈48,000 scores instead of 156{,}000 156,000. In training (width 256, batch 128, compiled) step time fell from 1.59 s to 1.18 s and peak memory from 18.7 GB to 16.4 GB, measured back to back. A test checks equality with the masked computation.

sec.title: Compilation and precision
sec.p: Compiling the training step with mx.compile cut step time by about 1.3× (1.22 s → 0.92 s at width 256, batch 128). Casting the generator to bfloat16 gave a further 1.4–1.8× in a first test but saved no memory, because the frozen fp32 codec promotes the generator’s inputs back to fp32; mixed precision is not used in the experiments reported here.

sec.title: Interrupted training and reproducibility
sec.p: Long runs need recoverable training state as well as model weights. Codec and generator snapshots now store optimizer moments and step, random state, shuffled-batch position, elapsed training time and model parameters; codec snapshots include VQ running averages and generator snapshots retain the best-validation model. Files are replaced atomically, with a preceding snapshot retained. A pause signal saves after the current step; a hard crash recovers from the last completed snapshot. Short CPU tests give identical saved state for uninterrupted and resumed training, including the compiled generator path. This does not establish equality across hardware or backends. Rented-pod recovery also depends on copying snapshots outside the container before it disappears.

E17 exposed the distinction: closing its terminal killed training after the last saved step, 30,000 of 32,000. That legacy checkpoint contained weights alone. Its continuation retains the learning-rate and batch positions but resets optimizer moments and random state, so it must be reported as a weights-only recovery. The recovered model solves 71.25 / 31.75 / 3.70% of easy/medium/hard boards, close to E13, after 2,000 continuation steps taking 1,247.53 s. This is consistent with puzzle construction affecting transfer, but the reset prevents a controlled causal conclusion. The operational procedure is documented in docs/RECOVERY.md.

sec.title: Experiments

disp-quote.p: In short. On a small invented language NCM is faster and somewhat less accurate than an AR model with similar generator size. On Sudoku our AR result is near the Original AR baseline; our NCM does not match Original NCM’s reported result.

sec.p: Runs use an Apple M5 Pro (64 GB unified memory, macOS 26.5), an RTX 3080 or a rented A40, as labelled for each experiment, with MLX 0.32.3. Other GPU workloads often ran on the Mac; timings this affects are marked.

sec.title: TinyWorld: an invented language
sec.p:
TinyWorld has 15,360 sentences of the form name verb count adjective noun, with number agreement (“one red cat”, “two red cats”), at most 32 characters. 12,000 sentences train the models; the rest are held out. A sentence is valid if it parses and agrees. The codec (6 levels,
l = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 l=1,2,4,8,16,32, 128 codes each, 1.3M parameters) rebuilds 100% of held-out sentences exactly. The NCM generator (5.0M parameters) is compared with a character-level AR transformer of the same width and depth (4.8M parameters) with a KV cache.

caption.p: TinyWorld, NCM and AR with similar generator size (E1); NCM also retains its codec.

tr.td: Valid and not in the training set, temperature 1.0

caption.p: Median latency per batch for NCM and AR models. Left: TinyWorld. Right: Sudoku. Both axes logarithmic.

sec.p:
NCM is less accurate and faster. Its errors are local spelling slips; agreement, a sentence-wide rule, holds in 99.8% of well-formed samples. Forcing the true codes for the first
k k levels and sampling the rest (E2) shows that errors arise at every level, not only the finest. Letting level
k k also read coarser levels (block-causal attention, E3) raised validity at temperature 1 from 89.8% to 92.2% (n = 1,024, standard error about 0.9 points) at 1.5–1.9× the latency.

sec.title: Sudoku
sec.p: Comparison labels. “MLX implementation” means the independently trained NCM model in this repository. “Original NCM” means Kumbong et al.’s published model and checkpoint results (Kumbong et al. 2026). The “MLX AR baseline” is trained here; the “Original AR baseline” is quoted from their study. The underlying method is NCM in both implementations.

Each board is 81 digits; the puzzle (blanks as 0) is the prefix and the solution is the target. Training uses 200,000 synthetic puzzles from randomised backtracking with 28–45 givens. Test sets are the 2,000 easy, medium and hard boards (40, 35 and 30 givens) published with the NCM paper. A board counts as solved if the output is a valid grid that keeps every given. Decoding is greedy.

caption.p: Sudoku, share of boards solved. Params counts generators only for NCM; the codec is additional. Paper rows are reference results from (Kumbong et al. 2026, Table 3). Budgets differ except for the explicitly matched E11 comparison.

tr.td: MLX AR baseline, E11’s budget (2M sequences)

sec.p: The first AR row is within a few percentage points of the Original AR baseline, but this numerical proximity does not establish a reproduction of its model or training recipe. Without conditioning corruption (E4–E6) our NCM solves nothing; with it (E8) it solves 6.2% of easy boards and fills 74.7% of blank cells correctly, more than the AR model’s 71.0%, while still solving fewer boards. E11 solves 55.2% of easy boards; at the same 2.048M generator presentations, the AR model solves 20.5%, 4.9% and 0.5%. This matches generator data exposure, not total training cost, FLOPs or system size. Section 8 records the changes.

The shared E6 codec contains 13,816,704 gradient-trained values, 49,152 EMA-trained codebook values and 49,344 EMA accumulators: 13,915,200 saved scalar values in total. Its learned first-level down/up convolutions account for 10,617,344 trainable values. The 6,440,128 generator values are additional; generator-size comparisons exclude the codec. Older rows preserve historical rounding; E15 and the newly completed runs retain their two-decimal solved rates. Each test set has 2,000 boards. Most recipes use one training seed; E19-funded and E20 provide two seeds of the same scientific recipe. Repeated sampling seeds do not quantify training variability.

Historical synchronized timings use temperature 1.0 while Sudoku quality uses greedy temperature 0.0. Both samplers remain uncompiled; mx.compile is used only for generator training when configured. Latency therefore does not directly time the solved-board decoding setting. The benchmark includes the output host copy, prefix work and final decoder, and records shared-device contention; cross-hardware timing ratios are not controlled comparisons.

Smaller-generator result. Easy-board accuracy is within 1.40 percentage points of Original NCM (98.10% versus 99.50%) with a 6.44M versus 25.46M generator: 3.95× smaller and 3.125× fewer generator presentations. This is a useful small-model result, not overall task parity: medium and hard remain 13.10 and 45.80 points behind. The separate codec is excluded from this size ratio, and the recipes and representation differ. E20 retains the same generator size and exposure but its easy score is 2.25 points below Original NCM; its medium/hard gaps are 16.90/52.85 points. The best-seed proximity on easy boards is not a reproducibility guarantee.

sec.title: Completed E18 and E19 experiments
sec.p: E18 tests stronger corruption on the base 200,000-puzzle corpus at E15’s 8.192M-presentation budget. Its 84.25 / 49.10 / 10.55% solve rates remain below both E14 and E15. Stronger corruption is therefore not a universal improvement, and this negative result remains part of the evidence.

The short E19 pilot uses the frozen E6 codec and 8M cached unique puzzles in addition to the base corpus. It completes 23,895 updates at batch 128 (3,058,560 presentations), solving 90.20 / 59.75 / 16.55%. E19-funded starts a fresh generator with the same corpus and a separate 128,000-update cosine schedule. At 16,384,000 presentations it solves 98.10 / 83.40 / 40.30%, improving on E15 by 1.85 / 6.75 / 8.40 percentage points. The exposure doubles while batch size, corpus and schedule differ. These comparisons establish outcomes of whole recipes, not a controlled effect of any one change.

caption.p: Completed training and checkpoint selection (training-loop seconds).

sec.p: The funded run completes its full schedule without a time-limit stop or optimizer reset; its final resumable snapshot is step 128,000, while held-out evaluation uses the best-validation step 127,000. Best weighted validation CE is 0.133244. The complete remote pipeline takes 55,700.91 s, including preprocessing, evaluation, benchmarking and transfer but excluding rental startup and the final cleanup wait. All 17 downloaded report/artifact files match their completion hashes. Source revision is 80dd445e5d17f54f53687a88459e011de4f9006f; the generator SHA-256 and full result extract are retained in the repository’s E19 report. Full-state snapshots preserve optimizer and random state; this uninterrupted run is not a test of cross-backend exact recovery.

Funded validation solves 70.90% of 1,000 boards. On easy/medium/hard tests, blank-cell accuracy is 99.69 / 97.12 / 86.99% and givens preservation is 100 / 100 / 99.60%; full-depth codec validation reconstruction is separately 100%. Wilson 95% intervals for the solved rates are 97.40–98.61 / 81.71–84.97 / 38.17–42.47%. These assume independent test boards, exclude training-seed variability and do not establish paired significance against prior runs. Per-board prediction archives were not retained. E20 supplies a second training seed below.

sec.title: E20: a second training seed
sec.p: E20 repeats the E19-funded scientific recipe with configured training seed 1 instead of 0. Both complete 128,000 updates at batch 128, using the frozen E6 codec, 200,000 base puzzles plus 8M cached unique puzzles, corruption 0.50→0.10, learning rate 0.0006 and 1,000-step warmup. Shared codec and corpus input-manifest hashes match. The configured seed affects initialization, minibatch order, dropout and corruption; internal generator streams use that seed plus one. These influences are not separately controlled.

The run name, output path and operational cap also change. E20’s cap is 960 rather than 1,440 minutes; neither run reaches its cap. E20 records no optimizer reset or truncation, and its final full-state snapshot and selected best checkpoint are both step 128,000. Training-loop time is 54,122.43 s; pipeline time is 55,543.62 s under the E19 timing boundary. Best weighted code CE is 0.142558, compared with 0.133244 for seed 0. Separate physical A40 allocations and missing remote source inventories prevent a strict same-host causal attribution.

caption.p: Two-seed held-out aggregates. Each seed reports the same 2,000-board benchmark per difficulty; the mean is descriptive, not a pooled independent sample.

sec.p: Both seeds retain strong easy-board performance and substantially weaker hard performance. E19-funded remains the best observed seed; neither two-seed means nor board-level Wilson intervals reliably estimate the population distribution of training outcomes. The intervals also exclude related-board dependence and repeated benchmark-guided recipe selection. Without per-board predictions, paired significance and agreement between the solved-board sets cannot be computed. No additional model evaluation is included in this version.

E20 validation solves 71.00%, compared with 70.90% for E19-funded, while hard blank-cell accuracy falls from 86.99% to 84.92%. Similar validation solving therefore does not imply similar external hard-set performance. The saved hard aggregates identify 670 valid grids, of which 665 preserve the givens: 1,330 failures are invalid grids and five additional failures are valid grids contradicting clues. Fourteen boards violate givens overall. Clue preservation alone cannot repair the dominant invalid-grid failure; the aggregates do not identify its internal cause.

Audit boundary. All 15 retained E20 completion files match recorded hashes; inference tensors equal the saved best-model tensors, and optimizer/training steps agree at 128,000. Generator SHA-256 is b6ddadb7278e7f1c5542eecef676840f39cb829e802d189b65f2dadd645c2b3d; the declared source is 4ad3646189197fe1ca76e45308848793fefe9a3f. These checks establish retained-byte integrity and internal consistency, not independent reproduction. No checkpoint-bound ordered scoring manifest, per-board predictions or remote source digest inventory was retained. Current local board files match the published hashes, but they were absent from the remote transfer-verification manifest. Actual remote evaluation identity, complete duplicate-free coverage and exact source bytes remain independently unverified. Reported outcomes are historical aggregates with these limits.

E20’s recorded synchronized benchmark uses temperature 1, three warmups and 20 iterations. Batch 1/16/64/256 p50 is 29.453/48.506/174.326/581.791 ms; p95 is 30.323/49.274/175.352/583.397 ms. The CUDA GPU-load log is empty because the wrapper used a Metal-only probe. Contention at benchmark time is unknown, and these timings neither measure greedy quality generation nor establish a seed-dependent speed effect.

Batch 1/16/64/256 p50 latency is 26.477 / 47.905 / 174.279 / 583.670 ms; p95 is 26.690 / 48.308 / 174.552 / 584.715 ms. This timing does not measure greedy quality decoding. Preflight records zero GPU utilization, zero allocated memory and no compute applications; an immediate pre-benchmark contention sample is not retained, so these are not certified idle-device limits. Neither cross-host A40 timings nor RTX 3080 comparisons isolate a hardware speed ratio.

The first funded allocation fails during shell preflight, before any training step, and is deleted. The failure is SIGPIPE from an early-closing version-check pipeline under pipefail; three regression cases reproduce it, and the corrected fresh attempt passes all 78 tests. Image startup timeouts recover before readiness. These are setup incidents, not extra training runs or reset-state continuations.

sec.p:
Why per-cell gains do not become solved boards. A board is about 300 codes. Teacher-forced accuracy per level in E6 ranges from 25% (level 0, which the puzzle barely determines) to 99.6% (the last level); generating greedily, an error at an early level changes the inputs of every later level. E8’s corruption training attacks exactly this compounding. Even 98% accuracy per cell, with independent errors, would solve only
0.98^{41} \approx 44\% 0.9841≈44% of easy boards, which have 41 blanks. The paper’s generator was trained on about 51 million sequences; E6 saw 0.5 million.

sec.title: A large chat model as reference
sec.p: Qwen3.8 27B (4-bit, served locally) answered each board in one request at temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. It solved none of 150 boards; its blank-cell accuracy was 11–15%, near chance, and about half its replies were not a 9 × 9 grid. With reasoning enabled and up to 6,000 tokens per board it did not finish ten boards in 95 minutes on the shared GPU. This is a reference point, not a matched comparison: the model is about 4,000 times larger and was not trained on the task.

sec.p: What the journey shows. The first Sudoku configuration failed for a reason no reconstruction test would reveal: its codec rebuilds boards perfectly yet places nearly all information in one level (the codec-refinement figure, E4), so the generator faces one large guess instead of a series of small ones. The fixes taken from upstream each helped a little and none was enough on its own. Reading the paper’s appendix in full showed the two largest gaps: conditioning corruption and a training budget about a hundred times larger. Corruption alone (E8) produced the first solved boards and lifted blank-cell accuracy by 20 points on every test set. Its validation loss was worse than without corruption, a reminder that teacher-forced loss does not measure what generation needs.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: What carries over to a laptop. Measured Apple Silicon runs show lower small-batch NCM latency than an AR model of similar generator size on the tested synthetic task. The advantage shrinks with batch size and code count; historical 12-level Sudoku generation is slower than AR from batch 64 on. These observations do not establish natural-text speed or isolate dispatch, memory traffic and kernel costs. The completed E19/E20 training runs use CUDA, not the Mac.

Partial success at the tested scale. A 6.44M generator learns substantial puzzle-conditioned structure: both funded-recipe seeds solve more than 97% of easy boards and 79% of medium boards. Both exceed E15’s reported rates, with twice its generator exposure and a changed overall recipe. This is sufficient evidence to continue studying the implementation. It is not an estimate of minimum required capacity, a scaling law or a demonstration of human-style logical reasoning. The additional codec prevents treating generator size as whole-system size.

Why hard Sudoku remains unresolved. The hard benchmark provides 30 clues, leaving 51 blanks, versus 40 clues and 41 blanks on easy boards. Every constraint and input clue must be satisfied simultaneously. Errors can be correlated, and a small change in average cell accuracy can accompany a larger change in exact-board accuracy. Neither clue count nor these aggregates reveals which logical dependencies the model fails to represent. The reference comparison also changes capacity, exposure, representation, corpus and difficulty-specific training. Those are candidate explanations, not experimentally established causes. Earlier width-512 trials do not justify promising that widening alone closes the gap.

How to challenge the interpretation. Before further long runs, retain checkpoint-bound input identities, per-board outputs and per-level diagnostics. Use a fresh untouched test set after fixing the selection protocol, since repeated examination of these benchmarks can guide recipe choices. Additional seeds characterize variation; separate random streams and controlled interventions are needed to identify whether initialization, order, dropout or corruption matters. True-code interventions on a diagnostic subset can test error propagation. Matched-data capacity and exposure ablations can test scale without conflating both. Checkpoint selection must use validation data rather than the external benchmark. These are proposed tests, not completed findings.

Decision for the next phase. The project can proceed to controlled text research without declaring the Sudoku reproduction complete. Keep the small generator as a reference while investigating independently converted Original NCM weights. Conversion parity would validate inference compatibility; it would not reproduce training or validate our smaller model. Begin text with a pinned permitted corpus, explicit tokenizer and padding boundaries, and document-separated splits. Report reconstruction and free-running generation separately, include readable failures and an autoregressive comparison with total-cost qualifications. Synthetic TinyStories would be an initial engineering benchmark; naturally occurring text and conditional tasks require further evidence. No instruction-following, summarization, translation or useful application integration follows from Sudoku scores.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Most generator recipes use at most 6.4M parameters; width-512 ablations use about 25M. E19-funded and E20 provide only two training seeds of one recipe, not a reliable population variance estimate. The best hard score remains 45.80 points below Original NCM; the second seed remains 52.85 points below. No current-budget AR comparison, matched total-cost study or natural-text validation is available. Full-depth codec validation reconstruction does not prove useful coarse representations under generated errors. Historical aggregate-only scoring, missing remote manifests, repeated benchmark-guided development and unknown benchmark contention limit independent audit and generalization. The original training implementation is not released; unstated recipe details remain uncertain. Existing measurements establish neither production reliability nor a benefit in a user application.

sec.title: Related work
sec.p: Parallel and coarse-to-fine decoding for text includes discrete diffusion (Sahoo et al. 2024) and the methods compared in (Kumbong et al. 2026). Residual quantisation is standard in audio codecs (Zeghidour et al. 2021) and image generation (Lee et al. 2022; Tian et al. 2024). Scheduled sampling (Bengio et al. 2015) addresses the train–test mismatch that conditioning corruption targets. Bakhaow/ncm-forge adds PyTorch training loops around upstream modules. The repository’s dated related-work comparison records other implementations; we make no priority claim for this MLX implementation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This independent MLX implementation preserves exact CPU training/per-level inference equivalence and demonstrates coarse-to-fine generation on a finite synthetic language and Sudoku. The funded small-generator recipe reports 97.25–98.10% easy, 79.60–83.40% medium and 33.25–40.30% hard solving across two seeds at equal exposure. We regard this as partial implementation and small-model success, with substantial failures on hard boards and unresolved provenance and reproducibility limits. It does not reproduce Original NCM’s scores or establish matched-cost superiority. The observed seed difference warrants better diagnostics rather than attributing the deficit to a single component. The next research phase will test text generation and its quality/cost tradeoff; those capabilities remain unvalidated.

sec.p: Later Sudoku runs reuse the frozen E6 codec and its 12-level, 16-code hierarchy. All use an 81-cell prefix, eight attention heads, configured generator seed 0 except E20 (seed 1), AdamW with weight decay 0.01, a cosine learning-rate schedule and compiled generator training. Generator dropout is 0.1 at width 256 and 0.2 at width 512; warmup is 200 steps at width 256 except E19/E20, which use 1,000; width 512 also uses 1,000. The codec is additional to the generator sizes below.

caption.p: Later Sudoku generator settings. Steps are completed steps for the reported results; corruption gives the first and last replacement probabilities.

sec.p: The base data are 200,000 training puzzles and 1,000 validation puzzles, with split seed 0 and 28–45 givens. E15 adds one million greedy-unique puzzles for each seed 201–204; E16 adds one million for each seed 205–206. E17 adds the unique subset of one million random-removal candidates for each seed 101–104; its final 2,000 steps are a weights-only continuation with reset optimizer and random state (Section 6.5). E12’s recorded run completed 50,776 steps; the repository’s current E12 configuration specifies 200,000, so running that configuration unchanged does not reproduce the reported exposure. E18 adds no unique-puzzle corpus. Both E19 runs and E20 add one million greedy-unique puzzles per seed 201–208; their separate schedules use full-state snapshots every 1,000 updates. The original million-step E19 configuration remains unstarted and is not either reported result. Full settings and checkpoint prerequisites are in the corresponding configs/sudoku-e*.json files and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md.
